books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, C. Workers and New Methods of Production
The North and the Textile Industry

stimulus.text: An engraving of the Boott Cotton Mills at Lowell, Massachusetts. Long brick mill buildings with rows of windows stand along a river, with smoking chimneys, a bridge, and small figures of workers and horse-drawn wagons in the foreground. The caption reads “BOOTT COTTON MILLS. LOWELL, MASS.”
stimulus.source_note: Engraving of the Boott Cotton Mills, Lowell, Mass., by Van Slyck & Co., Boston, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain). Image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The engraving best illustrates which feature of the factory system?

options.text: Workers made goods at home for merchants, paid by the piece
options.misconception: That is the putting-out system, the older way of making goods at home, not the factory system in the engraving.

options.text: Each mill produced only one part of a finished product
options.misconception: The Waltham-Lowell system put every stage of making cloth under one roof, not one part per mill.

options.text: All stages of making cloth came together under one roof
Mills were small workshops owned by the workers themselves
options.misconception: The engraving shows huge mill buildings owned by companies, with wage workers, not small shops owned by workers.

rationales.A: Home piecework for merchants is the putting-out system. The engraving shows the system that replaced it: large factory buildings.
rationales.B: Lowell mills spun yarn and wove cloth in the same place. The system gathered the stages together, it did not split them across mills.
rationales.C: The engraving shows vast mill buildings, not cottages or small shops. Under the Waltham-Lowell system, spinning, weaving, and finishing all happened in one place, with wage workers tending machines.
rationales.D: The buildings are company mills, far too large for a worker to own. The workers inside earned wages; they did not own the shops.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the scale. The buildings are huge, with rows of windows and smoking chimneys.
2. Ask what work fits that scale. Home piecework needs a cottage, not a mill like this.
3. Name the system. Lowell gathered every stage of making cloth under one roof.
Background: Slater's mill spun yarn; Lowell added power looms in 1813, so cloth was finished in the same mill.
Remember: when an image shows scale, ask what system needs that scale.
